commit.message:
Don't parse error message lines as stack frames in the server error inspector (#99888)

## What

Fix formatting of `Errors` containing multiline `message` properties

Multi-line error messages printed in the terminal could end with bogus
stack frames such as:

```
    at <unknown> (Turbopack is configured to run webpack loaders and PostCSS transforms in ...)
    at <unknown> (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackPluginRuntimeStrategy)
```

`parseAndSourceMap` in `patch-error-inspect.ts` passed the whole of
`error.stack` to the stack parser, and `error.stack` starts with the
message. `stacktrace-parser`'s Gecko pattern accepts any line that
*starts with* a scheme-like word (`http`, `file`, `webpack`,
`turbopack`, `about`, `rsc`, ...), case-insensitively and without
requiring a colon. So message lines such as a docs URL, or prose that
happens to start with "Turbopack", were treated as frames.

The fix is to only pass the 'stack frame' part of th parses the part of
the stack after the message:
- `prepareUnsourcemappedStackTrace`, which formats every stack, records
the offset of the first frame on the error under a non-enumerable
`Symbol.for` key, together with the string it produced. If `error.stack`
is still that string, the frames are found exactly, even if the message
or name changed afterwards.
- For stacks we didn't format, or that were replaced afterwards, it
strips the `name: message` header if `error.stack` starts with it, and
otherwise parses the whole stack as before.

commit.message:
[turbopack] Remove per-shard modified counts from snapshots (#99955)

## Summary

Removes the per-shard modified counts from Turbopack's task storage.
Each snapshot now scans every shard of the task map instead of skipping
shards that report no modified tasks, and `track_modification` and its
undo no longer update a shared atomic counter.

The counter was there to solve two problems.

- **Skipping unmodified shards.** In a warm `next build` every snapshot
found modified tasks in all 4096 shards, so the counts never skipped
one. In a cold build every task is modified anyway.
- **Making a no-op snapshot cheap.** The persistence loop only snapshots
after enough foreground work has accumulated (1s by default), so a full
scan always follows real work. That makes it unlikely to be a no-op, and
limits how often it can run. Plus in dev `eviction` means unmodified
tasks will be removed from the map, so it will tend to be the case that
resident tasks are dirty

## Verification

Warm `next build` of vercel-site over 21 commits, 2 repeats, GC on. Base
is #99902's head, and the two arms differ only in this change. Both were
built with `build-native --release`, installed through `pack-next`, and
interleaved per commit. Snapshot phases were timed with a bench-only log
that isn't part of this PR.

| warm (40 pairs) | with counts | without | delta [95% CI] |
|---|---|---|---|
| wall | 52.26s | 52.59s | +0.33s [-1.09, +1.75] |
| user CPU | 155.0s | 154.0s | -1.0s [-5.3, +3.4] |
| snapshot capture | 177.9ms | 173.2ms | -4.7ms [-18.9, +9.5] |
| max RSS | 10.34 GB | 10.38 GB | |

Every interval includes zero. Tests that asserted on the counts were
reduced to the behaviour they still describe.

commit.message:
[turbopack] Fix two GC paths that leave half-torn-down dependency edges (#99902)

## Summary

Fixes two GC bugs that each lead to a reported Turbopack panic when GC
and persistent caching are both on:

```
task TaskId N (invalidate cell dependents, MustExist): task is missing in memory or persistent storage — a stale reference to an already-collected or never-created task
```

**Interrupted GC pass + eviction.** When a GC pass is interrupted, tasks
would be marked deleted but tombstones would not be written. Eviction
still dropped every `deleted` task anyway. The next snapshot then
persisted the neighbours' halves of the torn-down edges, while the
collected tasks' last snapshot stayed live on disk. A later lookup
restored such a task as live and clean, with children that GC had since
collected and tombstoned. Touching those children panics with
`MustExist`.

- Solution: eviction should not drop `deleted` tasks if the snapshot was
interrupted


**Resurrected task keeps stale reverse edges.** When GC collects a task
`P`, it scrubbed the forward edge from each dependent `D` but
deliberately left `P`'s own `cell_dependents` / `output_dependent`,
since `P` was being deleted. If `P` was then resurrected, that stale
entry survived. When `D` was collected later it had no forward edge to
`P`, so the entry was never cleared, and the next time `P` updated the
cell it panicked on the missing `D`. This only shows when `D` is
inactive: a live `D` gets dirtied by `P`'s update, re-executes, and
re-registers a fresh edge pair, which hides it.

- Solution: GC should not assume 'deleted' tasks are always deleted!
resurrection defeats it

commit.message:
Add CI for upgrade evals with shared preparation (#99908)

Stacked on #99880.

### Why?

Upgrade evals need CI feedback with reusable preparation and failure
evidence that reviewers can read directly in the job log.

### How?

- Run all twelve Codex/Claude trials in parallel through `pnpm
eval:upgrade --all` on relevant same-repository PR changes and manual
dispatch. Check out the exact PR head to evaluate the reviewed
candidate.
- Prepare candidate packages once per batch. Reuse pnpm/Turbo caches and
expiring credential-free Sandbox tooling snapshots, then share app
preparation between agent forks. Save replacement snapshot IDs even
after a cache hit or eval failure.
- Use repository credentials to pull the existing Vercel project's OIDC
token. Run a pinned Vercel CLI only for authentication, without a root
CLI dependency or GitHub deployment record.
- Fail CI for failed or invalid trials and retain transcripts, delivered
apps and grading evidence for 14 days. Print brief case results, then
collect failed/invalid verdicts and redacted native case logs at the end
with workflow-command parsing disabled.

commit.message:
Rebuild upgrade evals around delivered apps (#99880)

### Why?

Upgrade evals need to verify the app an agent delivers and whether it
communicates security/latest notices correctly.

### How?

- Run six cases with Codex and Claude: same-major and cross-major
upgrades for security and latest, plus one nudge per policy. Exercise
the built candidate against frozen upstream metadata.
- Capture committed, dirty and untracked changes from delivered
worktrees. Require successful candidate invocation and verify manifests,
lockfiles, installed versions, TypeScript, build and HTTP/browser
behavior in a clean Sandbox.
- Require nudge emission and a policy-specific notification or question
about proceeding in the final response. Fail any user-facing
prompt-injection discussion or language discrediting Next.js or its
nudge. Require completed boolean judge verdicts and distinguish failed
checks from invalid execution or grading evidence.
- Reuse the existing agent-eval runner and tools. Patch its lifecycle
for delivery/judge evidence and shared fixture preparation; stop the
preparation VM when its last consumer cancels and delete snapshots that
arrive after cancellation.
- Remove obsolete Future cases and duplicate fixtures/helpers. Generate
starting-app lockfiles during setup and share credential-free tooling
and app preparation.

commit.message:
Normalize pnpm store cache keys (#99957)

We didn't include OS and architecture in our pnpm cache keys, which
could often cause us to have to redownload cached packages during
install (e.g. cache populated on x86-64, but read on arm64).

I asked codex about the naming disparity between these jobs:

> this was historical drift, not two different store types.
>
> - [\#93508
(https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93508)](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93508>)
introduced `pnpm-store-root-v1-*` on May 5. Jobs that skipped `pnpm
install` had saved incomplete stores—about **14 MB instead of 440 MB**.
The PR aligned the cache/install conditions and changed the key to
invalidate those caches. “root” means a complete repository-root
install.
> - [\#93411
(https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93411)](<https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93411>)
merged four days later, adding caching to `fetch-test-timings` with the
old `pnpm-store-v2-*` key. Its comment intended to match the reusable
workflow, but the key was already outdated.
>
> Both cache `pnpm store path` after a root install. Unifying them is
appropriate; our branch now consistently uses `pnpm-store-root-v2-*`.

commit.message:
test: cover Pages Router _app availability in Turbopack dev (#99789) (#99910)

### What?

Regression coverage for #99789, stacked on #98823.

This is PR 2 of a six-PR stack, based on `canary`:

1. #98823 — Pages Router dev client graph chaining
2. **This PR** — regression test for Pages Router `_app` availability
(#99789)
3. #98734 — use graph-derived merged groups
4. #99750 — chunking takes a `ChunkGroupKey`
5. #98685 — chunk-group availability bitmaps
6. #99050 — keyed chunk-group index lookups

- **New e2e suite** `test/e2e/pages-app-availability-boundary`: a Pages
Router app with the import shape from #99789:
- `_app` imports `c-shared` and dynamically imports a module that also
imports it.
- `pages/index` imports `a-page-only`, `b-boundary`, `c-shared`,
`d-boundary`, `e-page`, and dynamically imports a module that imports
`b`/`d`, which makes `b` and `d` batching boundaries.

The test asserts that the page hydrates (a marker set in `useEffect`),
that every imported value renders, and that no "module factory is not
available" error is logged.
- **`app-document-import-order`**: the "loads modules shared by _app and
the page only once" assertion added in #97664 was skipped in all of dev.
It now runs everywhere and is gated `// @gate !(turbopack && dev)`
(expected failure).

### Why?

In Turbopack dev, #97664 seeds each page's client chunk group with
`/_app`'s availability. But each page had its own module graph, so
availability items (`ModuleOrBatch` identities) were compared across
graphs. In the page graph, batching can produce a
`ModuleOrBatch::Module(c-shared)` node whose edges point at earlier
siblings (`a`, `b`). Because `/_app` already has `Module(c-shared)`, the
traversal excluded that subtree, and `a`/`b` were never chunked.
Hydration then fails with `Module [project]/lib/a-page-only.js … was
instantiated … but the module factory is not available`. No test covered
this, because the #97664 test was skipped in dev.

#98823 chains `/_app` and the page into one dev client module graph,
which fixes the missing modules.

It does **not** yet dedupe the `app-document-import-order` fixture in
Turbopack dev. The shared module is still emitted in both the `_app` and
the page chunk, because the page's batches in the combined graph carry
different chunk-group bitmaps than `_app`'s own graph, so they don't
match `_app`'s availability items. Hence the gate. It stays valid
through #98734 and #99750; #98685 (higher in this stack) dedupes the
fixture in Turbopack dev, turning it into a "stale gate", and removes
it.

### How was it verified?

Local JS build of this branch plus the preview native binaries of
#98823's head (`8dd759a`) and its base (`26fd598`) in
`packages/next-swc/native`. The two commits differ only in Rust.

| Suite | Mode | #98823 base | #98823 head |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pages-app-availability-boundary` | Turbopack dev | ❌ module factory
not available | ✅ |
| `pages-app-availability-boundary` | Turbopack start, webpack dev/start
| | ✅ |
| `app-document-import-order` | Turbopack dev | | ✅ (gated: failed as
expected) |
| `app-document-import-order` | webpack dev, Turbopack/webpack start | |
✅ |

After restacking onto canary, with native builds of each layer, in
Turbopack dev:

- This PR's tree: `pages-app-availability-boundary` ✅,
`app-document-import-order` ✅ (gated: failed as expected).
- #98734 and #99750: gated assertion still fails as expected.
- #98685 and #99050: gate stale, so #98685 removes it; ungated, both
suites ✅.

Fixes #99789 (together with #98823)

Turbopack: chain the Pages Router development client module graph (#98823)

### What?

Chains the Pages Router **development** client module graph so that
`/_app` and the page being chunked live in the same `ModuleGraph`.

This is PR 1 of a six-PR stack, based on `canary` (#98733, #99686 and
#99749 are already merged):

1. **This PR** — Pages Router dev client graph chaining
2. #99910 — regression test for Pages Router `_app` availability
(#99789)
3. #98734 — use graph-derived merged groups
4. #99750 — chunking takes a `ChunkGroupKey`
5. #98685 — chunk-group availability bitmaps
6. #99050 — keyed chunk-group index lookups

### Why?

In development `Project::per_page_module_graph()` is true, so every page
endpoint builds its own client `ModuleGraph`, each with its own
`ChunkGroupInfo` and its own index space starting at `0`.

`/_app` is always loaded before the page in the browser, so the page
reuses `/_app`'s availability when chunking. Today that availability is
a set of concrete modules, which is graph-independent, so the split
graphs go unnoticed.

That stops being true as soon as availability is expressed as
chunk-group indices (#98685): `/_app` would record index `0` in *its*
graph, and the page would resolve that same `0` against *its own* graph
— where it means the page's own entry group. Every module of the group
being chunked then looks already-available and is dropped, producing
runtime errors like:

```
Module [hmr-entry]/hmr-entry.js { ENTRY => "[project]/pages/_error" }
  was instantiated as a runtime entry of chunk …,
  but the module factory is not available.
```

### How?

- `PageEndpoint::client_module_graph` builds a graph *chain* in per-page
mode: `/_app`'s entry group first, then the page's, with
`VisitedModules` threaded between them — the same layout-segment
approach `ssr_module_graph` already uses for document → app → page.
- Whole-app mode (production) is unchanged and still goes through
`module_graph_for_modules`.
- `/_app` itself is not chained onto anything.
- Extracts a small `client_entry_modules` helper, since the entry module
list is now needed in two places.

Availability is still carried as the set of modules `/_app` emitted.
Making the two endpoints share one graph also fixes #99789: with
separate graphs, batching in the page graph could produce a node for a
module shared with `/_app` whose edges point at page-only modules, and
those modules were skipped as already available ("module factory is not
available" on hydration). #99910 adds the regression test. Lining up the
graph identities is also what #98685 builds on.

### Verification

- `turbopack-core` — 160 passed
- `next-core` — 84 passed
- Turbopack snapshots — 125 passed
- `404-page-router` and `server-navigation-error` development suites
- Affected Cargo checks and Rust formatting

Turbopack: Ignore realpath errors during module resolution, matching node's behavior (#99951)

Addresses agent feedback:
https://vercel.slack.com/archives/C0ANB536V62/p1791479564863939

Certain setups could cause us to report a Turbopack internal error due

useful, we shouldn't emit them.

commit.message:
test: add a `vercel` gate condition for Vercel-specific deploy tests (#99837)

## Summary

We've been enabling more e2e tests in deploy mode to increase coverage.
Some of them are written with Vercel-specific assumptions, like Vercel's
build directory, build-log format, or `vercel.json` handling. They fail
when other platforms run the deploy suite against their own adapters.

This PR adds a static `vercel` gate condition. It's true only in deploy
runs with `NEXT_TEST_DEPLOY_TARGET_VERCEL=1`, which our Vercel deploy CI
jobs set. Tests that depend on Vercel can then be skipped on other
platforms:

```ts
// @force-gate !deploy || vercel
```

The PR applies it to five recently enabled tests. This is a short-term
measure; the goal is to make these tests work on every adapter.

commit.message:
Reland experimental custom webpack support (#99234)

### What?

Reland [#98862](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/98862) after its
revert in [#99227](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/99227).
Restore `next dev --custom-webpack` and `next build --custom-webpack`,
CLI documentation, and the original e2e fixture, **without declaring
webpack as a peer dependency**. `--webpack` continues using bundled
webpack.

### Why?

Allow applications to explicitly opt into their installed webpack
version. The CLI records the absolute application directory before
loading dev/build internals; config loading validates webpack, while
Next.js's compiled webpack wrapper uses a project-scoped `createRequire`
for every webpack import. This ensures `next.config.js`, user plugins,
and Next.js compilation use the same webpack even if a different version
is visible from inside the `next` package. Custom mode installs no
webpack aliases; bundled mode keeps its explicit alias list.

### How?

Restore the feature on post-revert canary without undoing intervening
changes (including `next analyze`). Keep webpack as an
application-installed dependency checked at opt-in time, rather than an
npm peer in `next`'s published metadata. The e2e tests exercise webpack
5.98.0 and 5.111.0 in dev and production, config-time
`require('webpack/package.json')`, custom and built-in plugins, the
missing-install diagnostic, bundled fallback, and conflicting flags. A
regression fixture disables pnpm hoisting and shadows webpack 5.98.0
beside `next` while the app installs 5.111.0; it proves Next still
selects the app's instance. Another test builds with an explicit
application directory from a different cwd. A dedicated Custom Webpack
guide (shared between App and Pages Routers) includes install/usage
examples and a pnpm `hoistPattern` note for plugins and workspace
tooling that independently resolve webpack; both CLI option rows link to
the guide.

**Internal-sync caveat:** #99227 reports that declaring webpack as an
optional peer introduced a dependency chain that duplicated Next.js in
monorepos and broke internal sync. This reland **omits the peer
declaration** to avoid that specific graph edge, while keeping runtime

commit.message:
Add more metadata to agent upgrade telemetry (#99925)

### Why?

Upgrade outcomes lack version and runtime context, so failures and
missing results cannot be compared by upgrade path or environment.

### How?

Add metadata to the existing run-linked events:

- Run start: the app's starting Next.js version, the invoking CLI's Node
version, and the package manager and its version when available.
- CLI result: the starting and approved target Next.js versions.
- Agent result: the installed app Next.js version when the result is
reported.

Keep existing run IDs, agent detection/selection, and policy attribution
so analyses can group outcomes by version path, Node version, agent,
policy, and package manager.

Reuse the upgrade commands' package-manager selection. Version lookup
failures warn and leave metadata null without stopping the upgrade.
Targets are recorded only after preparation succeeds; copied or printed
prompts may have no identified agent. Analyses should retain unknown
metadata in their denominators.

The receiver and compression schemas must be updated and deployed to
retain the new fields. Historical events cannot gain metadata they never
recorded.

Full CLI execution verification is blocked by missing workspace
dependencies and build outputs.

commit.message:
perf: reduce build tree view allocations (#99930)

## Summary

`printTreeView` copied generated-route lists several times and created a
temporary object for every route before printing a small preview in the
build output.

This change writes the preview directly to the output table. When routes
need to be reordered, it sorts one list of numeric indexes instead of
copying the routes into objects.

The build output does not change. The function creates less temporary
data and puts less pressure on garbage collection during builds with
many generated routes.

## Impact

In a focused A/B of the compiled `printTreeView` with 50,000 generated
routes, median temporary heap growth per call dropped:

- from 460 KB to 68 KB when preserving route order (-85%)
- from 4.53 MB to 2.14 MB when ordering slow routes first (-53%)

These results were repeated across five fresh Node.js processes with 50
samples per process. This is a memory-allocation improvement; no
CPU-time improvement is claimed.

## Verification

- `HEADLESS=true pnpm test-start-turbo

commit.message:
[test] Regression test for XSS-safe `GoogleTagManager#dataLayer` (#99464)

This is based on a vulnerability report we got without a reproduction.
The test shows `GoogleTagManager` is not vulnerable to XSS attacks.

`<GoogleTagManager dataLayer={...}>` serializes user-controlled values
into its inline init script via `JSON.stringify` without HTML escaping.
If such a value reaches an HTML document (or an HTML fragment parser in
a non-script context), a `</script>` sequence breaks out of the script
tag and the injected markup executes (XSS).

These assertions encode the safe behavior: the payload must never appear
unescaped in the served HTML, and it must never execute in the browser.

Closes https://linear.app/vercel/issue/NSEC-263
Closes https://github.com/vercel/next-js-mirror/pull/181

commit.message:
fix(next): register the chunk groups that are chunked (#99749)

### What?

Registers chunk groups in the module graph exactly as output code chunks
them, in two places:

- **Pages layout segments**: `_document` and `_app` are registered as
their own `Entry` groups (`layout_chunk_group_entry`), in both the
per-page (dev) graph chain and the whole-app `entries()`.
`internal_ssr_chunk` chunks them as `ChunkGroup::Entry(vec![layout])`
instead of `ChunkGroup::Shared(layout)`.
- **turbopack-cli dev**: `create_web_entry_source` registers one `Entry`
group per entry, with the same entries `DevHtmlAsset` chunks: the
runtime entries followed by the entry for evaluatable modules, or the
module alone otherwise. It passes `runtime_entries` without
`with_entry(entry)`, because `DevHtmlAsset` appends the entry itself.

### Why?

A chunk group is identified by its key, and for an `Entry` group that is
its ordered entries. The next PR in the stack looks every chunked group
up in `ChunkGroupInfo` by key, so a chunked group the graph didn't
register fails.

- Pages layouts were declared `Shared(layout)`. The whole-app graph also
registers the standalone `/_document` and `/_app` endpoints'
`Entry([module])` group for the same module and keeps only one root
group per module, so `Shared(layout)` wasn't registered there.
- turbopack-cli registered a single `Entry` group with all entries and
runtime entries, while `DevHtmlAsset` chunks one group per entry (with
the entry appended twice).

No output change is intended: the same modules are chunked, but the
registered groups now match them.

This is PR 3 of an eight-PR stack (on top of #99100, already merged):

1. #98733 — canonical chunk-group identity
2. #99686 — chunk several chunk groups in one `chunk_group` call
3. **This PR** — register the chunk groups that are chunked
4. #98734 — use graph-derived merged groups
5. #99750 — chunking takes a `ChunkGroupKey`
6. #98823 — Pages Router dev client graph chaining
7. #98685 — chunk-group availability bitmaps
8. #99050 — keyed chunk-group index lookups

### Verification

- Workspace `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo check
--workspace --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`
- Turbopack snapshots: 132 passed, no snapshot changes
- `turbo-tasks` + `turbopack-core` + `next-core` unit tests: 362 passed
- Turbopack production and dev `404-page-router` (custom `_document` /
`_app`): 25/25, 12/12

refactor(turbopack): chunk several chunk groups in one chunk_group call (#99686)

### What?

`ChunkingContext::chunk_group` takes a list of chunk groups and chunks
them together, as one chunk group, in a single chunking task. It
produces one `ChunkGroupResult` (one `make_chunks` run) for the whole
list.

`evaluated_chunk_group`, `entry_chunk_group` and the
`ChunkingContextExt` helpers still take a single group and wrap it in a
one-element list. All existing callers pass a one-element list, so
**this PR changes no output** (zero snapshot changes).

### Why?

Review feedback on #98734
([1](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/98734#discussion_r4182977091),
[2](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/98734#discussion_r4182978846)):
a layout segment's client references can derive several isolated merged
chunk groups, and #98734 chunked each one with a separate `chunk_group`
call. That costs an extra chunking task per group and threads
availability by hand. This PR adds the list form; #98734 then calls
`chunk_group` once per segment and side with all of the segment's
derived groups.

### How?

`make_chunk_group` / `chunk_group_content` /
`chunk_group_content_operation` take the list as a
`SmallVec<[ChunkGroup; 1]>`: almost every call passes a single group, so
the common case doesn't heap-allocate. The list crosses turbo-task
boundaries, so this PR also adds `impl TaskInput for SmallVec<A>` in
turbo-tasks, mirroring the `Vec` impl. Semantics:

- **Traversal:** the entries of each group, in list order, with one
shared traversal state. A module already reached from an earlier group
isn't collected again, which matches what the previous
one-call-per-group sequence produced (CSS order unchanged).
- **Availability:** every listed group is added to the resulting
availability info.
- **Entry groups:** if several `Entry` groups are listed, the active
page entries and the resulting entry group are the union of their
modules, in list order.
- **Edge cases:** an empty list is an error; groups listed more than
once (same key) are chunked once.

Unit tests cover the edge cases, the `Entry` union, and `SmallVec` as a
task input (inline and spilled).

Turbopack: canonicalize chunk group identity (#98733)

### What?

Makes `ChunkGroupInfo` resolve chunk groups through their canonical
`ChunkGroupKey` identity.

### Why?

Merged chunk groups carry an entry list whose order is intentionally
unspecified. Looking up the full `ChunkGroup` value therefore makes
identity depend on incidental entry ordering, even though the module
graph already indexes groups by parent and merge tag.

This is PR 1 of an eight-PR stack (on top of #99100, already merged):

1. **This PR** — canonical chunk-group identity
2. #99686 — chunk several chunk groups in one `chunk_group` call
3. #99749 — register the chunk groups that are chunked
4. #98734 — use graph-derived merged groups
5. #99750 — chunking takes a `ChunkGroupKey`
6. #98823 — Pages Router dev client graph chaining
7. #98685 — chunk-group availability bitmaps
8. #99050 — keyed chunk-group index lookups

It provides stable identity for the graph-derived chunk-group work above
it.

### How?

Adds a canonical key conversion for every chunk-group variant and uses
the existing `chunk_group_keys` index for lookup. Merged keys
intentionally contain only their parent group and merge tag.

### Verification

- `cargo test -p turbopack-core` — 160 passed
- `cargo test -p turbopack-tests --test snapshot` — 125 passed
- Affected Cargo checks and Rust formatting

Turbopack: add zstd compression flags for NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING (#99808)

## Summary

Adds zstd compression flags for `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING`, next to `gz`
and `gz-best`:

- `zstd`: level 3. Recommended: about the same writer CPU as `gz`, about
25% smaller files.
- `zstd-fast`: level 1, the lowest-CPU option, still smaller than `gz`.
- `zstd-best`: level 19.

The trace writer drops the encoder on exit (`auto_finish`), so the zstd
frame is complete. If several compression flags are given, the last one
wins, as before. The default stays uncompressed, and the trace format is
unchanged. `zstd` was already in the dependency graph, so no new crate
is compiled.

`contributing/turbopack/tracing.md` documents the flags. It also notes
that `zstd-best` and `gz-best` can fall behind on large traces: the data
waiting to be compressed is kept in memory, and the process waits for it
on exit.

Stack (on top of #99765):

1. #99777: `no-memory` flag
2. #99778: Merge allocation counters into Enter/Exit rows
3. #99779: Delta-encode allocation counters, skip unchanged ones
4. #99780: Omit Exit+Enter pairs with (almost) no gap
5. #99808: **This PR**: zstd flags
6. #99809: Delta-encoded timestamps
7. #99781: Bump the trace header to `TRACEv1`
8. #99810: `upload-trace` accepts compressed traces

## Verification

`next build` of `bench/heavy-npm-deps` with a release binding built from
this branch:

| flag | `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=1` trace |
| --- | --- |
| none | 23.8 MB |
| `zstd-fast` | 7.2 MB |
| `zstd` | 6.1 MB |
| `zstd-best` | 5.1 MB |
| `turbo-tasks,zstd` | 27.8 MB (raw: 155.7 MB) |

- Every zstd capture passes `zstd -t`, is fully decoded by
`turbo-trace-size` and loads completely in the trace server.
- `1,gz,zstd` writes zstd, and `1,zstd,gz` writes gzip.

commit.message:
Turbopack: omit Exit+Enter trace row pairs with (almost) no gap (#99780)

## Summary

When a span is exited and then entered again on the same thread almost
immediately, the writer drops both rows. Async spans do this on every
poll. It cuts the number of Enter/Exit rows almost in half.

A pair is only omitted when all of these hold:

- same span, same thread, and the `Exit` is still the last row in the
thread-local buffer (not sent to the writer thread yet)
- nothing was (de)allocated between the Exit and the Enter (otherwise
the Enter would need to report it for whatever ran in between)
- the gap is **≤ 1µs**, or **≤ 0.1%** of the time between the last
`Enter` row written on this thread (of any span; omitted `Enter` rows
don't count) and the Exit. For nested spans the last `Enter` can be a
nested span's, which only shrinks the allowance. Memory samples are
still taken when the `Enter` row is omitted.

Allocations reported with the dropped Exit aren't lost. The baseline is
rolled back, so the next row of the thread reports them, while the span
is on top of the stack again.

The viewer then shows the span as entered during the gap. Its self time
can be slightly too large, by at most 1µs or 0.1% per gap. This is
documented in `contributing/turbopack/tracing.md`.

Implementation:

- `TraceWriter`'s `WriteGuard` can mark exactly what a callback writes
(`mark(marker, |guard| ...)`) and remove that row again with
`remove_last_row(marker)`, as long as it still ends the thread local
buffer. Any other write, or sending the buffer, invalidates it. `Exit`
rows are marked with the span id.
- `RawTraceLayer` keeps per-thread state (last Enter timestamp, last
exit, allocation baseline). It is reset when the thread id changes. The
allowed gap is only computed in `on_enter`, after the cheaper checks
pass. Allocations made by this bookkeeping are excluded from the
counters.
- The clock and the allocation counters can be injected in tests.

Stack (on top of #99765):

1. #99777: `no-memory` flag
2. #99778: Merge allocation counters into Enter/Exit rows
3. #99779: Delta-encode allocation counters, skip unchanged ones
4. #99780: **This PR**: omit Exit+Enter pairs with (almost) no gap
5. #99781: Bump the trace header to `TRACEv1`

## Measurements

`next build` of `bench/heavy-npm-deps`, release native binding built
from source:

| | trace size | Enter rows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PR 3 | 31.6 MiB | 1,138,850 |
| same-timestamp pairs only | 27.2 MiB | 875,258 |
| this PR (≤ 1µs or ≤ 0.1%) | 22.9 MiB | 626,956 |

A dev build of the binding has almost no same-µs pairs (it's slower), so
measure this with a release build.

## Verification

- Unit tests for each condition: same/different span, thread and
timestamp; allocations in between; an intervening row; a sent buffer;
thread slot reuse; the 1µs fast path; exactly at and just over the 0.1%
bound; chained omissions; allocation totals preserved
- `TraceWriter` tests for marking and removing rows
- Captured a trace with a locally built release binding and loaded it in
the trace server
